summary.title: An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT homogenization
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a novel algorithm to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient histories in non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. Traditional FFT methods typically impose strain control, requiring iterative corrections for stress or mixed loading, which increases computational cost. The authors introduce a modified projection operator where the null frequency enforces the specific control type (stress or strain) for each component of the macroscopic first Piola stress or deformation gradient. This modification allows the problem to be solved exactly as the original variational method without additional iterations in the linear solver or Newton scheme. The method is demonstrated through numerical examples involving a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material and a polycrystal. For the hyperelastic case, the algorithm shows identical convergence rates and simulation times compared to strain control. For the polycrystal, which exhibits rate-dependent behavior, the stress-controlled case is faster due to elastic increments, while the pseudo-uniaxial strain control yields inaccurate transverse stresses compared to true stress control. The study confirms that the proposed method preserves the computational efficiency of FFT homogenization while enabling accurate simulation of generic loading paths, including uniaxial tension and controlled triaxility, without the overhead of iterative load corrections.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a novel algorithm to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient histories in non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. Traditional FFT methods typically impose strain control, requiring iterative corrections for stress or mixed loading, which increases computational cost. The authors introduce a modified projection operator where the null frequency enforces the specific control type (stress or strain) for each component of the macroscopic first Piola stress or deformation gradient. This modification allows the problem to be solved exactly as the original variational method without additional iterations in the linear solver or Newton scheme. The method is demonstrated through numerical examples involving a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material and a polycrystal. For the hyperelastic case, the algorithm shows identical convergence rates and simulation times compared to strain control. For the polycrystal, which exhibits rate-dependent behavior, the stress-controlled case is faster due to elastic increments, while the pseudo-uniaxial strain control yields inaccurate transverse stresses compared to true stress control. The study confirms that the proposed method preserves the computational efficiency of FFT homogenization while enabling accurate simulation of generic loading paths, including uniaxial tension and controlled triaxility, without the overhead of iterative load corrections.

Research Context
Computational homogenization simulates mechanical response in a periodic representative volume element. The finite element method traditionally solves boundary value problems with any load history. FFT-based homogenization is a popular alternative due to computational performance. Imposing macroscopic stress or mixed loading is not direct in standard FFT. Classical schemes require a reference medium which affects convergence. Iterative approaches for stress control significantly increase iteration counts. Galerkin-based FFT uses weak formulation and projection operators. Previous variational approaches only imposed macroscopic deformation gradient history.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to extend the variational algorithm for finite strains. The goal is to use stress and mixed control of macroscopic load. The method uses a direct approach based on a modified projection operator. The hypothesis is that computational performance of the original method is preserved. The algorithm should not require additional iterations compared to strain control. The method applies to both linear iterative solvers and Newton schemes. The approach allows solving problems with mixed boundary conditions efficiently.

Methodological Details
The RVE is discretized in nx ny nz voxels. The linear momentum balance is imposed in its weak form. Test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projector. The projection operator enforces compatibility of strain fields. The Helmholtz decomposition splits tensor fields into compatible and incompatible parts. The standard projection operator is zero at null and Nyquist frequencies. For stress control, a modified operator G* is defined. The null frequency of G* is the fourth order identity tensor. This enforces the average stress to equal the target macroscopic stress. For mixed control, the operator varies by component direction. Stress-controlled components use the identity tensor at null frequency. Strain-controlled components use zero tensor at null frequency. The non-linear system is solved using Newton iteration. The linear system is solved using the conjugate gradient method.

Procedures And Architectures
The first benchmark is a particle reinforced hyperelastic matrix. The RVE contains 4 particles with a volume fraction of 0.2. The domain is discretized using 643 voxels. The matrix follows a Saint Venant-Kirchhoff hyperelastic model. Matrix shear modulus is 28 Pa and bulk modulus is 46.67 Pa. Particles are one order of magnitude stiffer than the matrix. The uniaxial tensile test reaches an elongation of 0.2. Load is divided into 100 load increments. Case 1 is mixed control with strain ramp in x direction. Case 2 is full stress control with a linear ramp. Case 3 is full strain control with a linear ramp. The second benchmark is a polycrystal with 200 grains. The polycrystal uses a crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic model. A final elongation of 0.02 is imposed in 200 seconds. Time is discretized in 20 regular increments. Case 4 is a pseudo-uniaxial test using full strain control.

Key Results
In the hyperelastic case, cases 1 and 2 share the same path. Macroscopic stress for cases 1 and 2 are superposed. Case 3 follows a slightly different path due to full strain control. Transverse stresses are zero under stress and mixed control. Small compressive transverse stresses develop under strain control. Macroscopic and microscopic results at the endpoint are identical within accuracy. In the polycrystal, cases 1 and 2 are not exactly superposed. Differences arise due to strain rate effects in the visco-plastic model. Case 4 pseudo-uniaxial test shows non-zero compressive transverse stresses. These transverse stresses grow with applied strain in case 4. Stress and mixed controlled simulations took similar iterations to strain control. Hyperelastic simulations needed almost identical times for every boundary condition. Polycrystal case 2 is faster due to elastic increments. Convergence criteria for linear solver is L2 norm of residual. Tolerances are 10^-8 for linear and 10^-6 for Newton solvers.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The modified projection operator allows direct imposition of stress control. This avoids the iterative correction of strain in classical schemes. The method preserves the efficiency of the Galerkin-based FFT framework. It enables accurate simulation of uniaxial and mixed loading paths. The results show that pseudo-uniaxial strain control can be inaccurate. True stress control is necessary for accurate transverse response in plastic materials. The algorithm is general and applicable to any material model.

Contradictions And Limitations
The method requires defining the modified operator for each control type. For rate-dependent materials, stress control may lead to different paths. The study uses fixed time steps, which may affect adaptive stepping. The polycrystal example shows that pseudo-uniaxial strain control is inaccurate. The method assumes periodic boundary conditions on the RVE.

Claims
The proposed algorithm imposes stress or mixed control without additional iterations. The method does not require additional iterations. Convergence rate is the same as the original scheme. Polycrystal case 2 is faster, but this is due to elastic steps. It allows efficient simulation of generic loading paths.
Pseudo-uniaxial strain control leads to inaccurate transverse stresses in plastic materials. Compressive transverse stresses are not zero in case 4. These stresses grow with applied strain. In hyperelastic materials, endpoint results are identical. True stress control is required for accurate plastic response.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The method was tested on hyperelastic and crystal plasticity models. Performance was compared across strain, stress, and mixed control. Convergence behavior was analyzed for each time increment.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the particle reinforced RVE and stress responses. Figure 2 shows the polycrystalline RVE and stress responses. Figure 3 compares convergence and simulation times.

Three Takeaways
1. A modified projection operator enables direct stress and mixed control in FFT homogenization. 2. The method preserves computational efficiency, requiring no extra iterations. 3. True stress control is essential for accurate simulation of plastic materials.
